per_claim.notes: ANI of all four Lebanese isolates vs N. gonorrhoeae FA1090 is ~83.6–85.2%, far below the 95% species boundary, supporting reclassification away from gonorrhoeae. R20 clusters with mucosa at 96.06% ANI; the other three are clearly in the non-pathogenic oral Neisseria cluster rather than gonorrhoeae/meningitidis.

R20= N. mucosa is supported (96.06% to mucosa reference). However, labeling R19/R21/R23 as N. flavescens is not supported under the stated 95% ANI rule: their best matches are to perflava/subflava references (e.g., R19 is 98.04–98.05% to subflava/perflava genomes), and pairwise ANI among R19/R21/R23 includes <95% values (94.32, 94.58), inconsistent with a single-species assignment as flavescens by strict ANI.

Only ANI was recomputed (with skani, a valid ANI estimator). isDDH and pangenome were not rerun, so the paper’s 'best approach isDDH+ANI+pangenome' and the joint boundary framing (95% ANI / 70% dDDH) were not independently validated beyond applying the 95% ANI threshold.

The provided ANI matrix shows at least one clear NCBI label/content mismatch: VK64 deposited as 'N. sicca' is ~96.83% ANI to N. macacae (ATCC33926), indicating mislabeling. The replication’s own spot-check conclusion for VK64 was incorrect because it used the wrong best hit; using the matrix, the misclassification signal is strong.

ANI results show substantial boundary ambiguity within the flavescens/perflava/subflava/mucosa complex: Lebanese 'flavescens' isolates are closer to perflava/subflava than to a flavescens type/reference, and some isolate–isolate ANIs fall just below 95%. This supports the paper’s broader point about taxonomic ambiguity in this group.

surprising_findings: R19 shows very high ANI to N. subflava/perflava references (98.04–98.05%) but only 94.08% to a flavescens reference (ATCC13120), contradicting a clean flavescens assignment under a 95% ANI rule.
R19/R21/R23 are not mutually ≥95% ANI (two pairwise comparisons are <95%), which is unexpected if all three are the same species by the paper’s stated cutoff.
The replication’s VK64 check was misinterpreted: the ANI matrix indicates VK64’s best match is N. macacae (~96.8%), not mucosa.
what_missing: No independent recomputation of isDDH (GGDC) values; therefore the 70% dDDH boundary and combined-method concordance were not directly tested.
No pangenome/Roary (or equivalent) rerun; thus the pangenome-based clustering/support for species calls was not replicated.

Limited reference sampling (15 references) may affect nearest-neighbor species calls within a highly ambiguous complex; a denser panel of curated type strains/genomes could change 'best match' conclusions.
No replication of MALDI-TOF results; only genome-based evidence was assessed.
justification: This replication substantially supports the core WGS-vs-API message that the Lebanese isolates are not N. gonorrhoeae (all are ~84–85% ANI to FA1090) and robustly confirms R20 as N. mucosa (96.06% ANI). It also provides evidence consistent with NCBI taxonomic mislabeling (VK64 labeled N. sicca but ~96.8% ANI to N. macacae) and reinforces the paper’s claim of genuine ambiguity within the flavescens/perflava/subflava/mucosa complex. However, the specific claim that R19/R21/R23 are N. flavescens is not reproduced under the paper’s own 95% ANI species boundary, and key components of the paper’s preferred multi-tool approach (isDDH and pangenome) were not rerun, so overall the replication is best judged as PARTIAL rather than fully replicated or contradicted.
